title: The Offer to Karna
story:
Of all the men on that field, the one Krishna sought out was the one who could still change the war.

The armies had met at Kurukshetra: the five Pandava brothers and their hundred cousins the Kauravas, who had robbed them of their kingdom. The great teaching was over. Krishna, cousin and charioteer of the Pandava prince Arjuna, had spoken it, and Arjuna's doubts had fallen away. When Arjuna took up his great bow Gandiva once more, the Pandava warriors raised a tremendous shout. They blew their conches, great shells from the sea that sounded like trumpets; drums and cow-horns joined in, and the noise rolled across the field. Even the gods came to watch, and with them the Gandharvas and the Pitris, the hosts of Siddhas and Charanas, and the blessed Rishis, Indra the king of the gods at their head.

Then, before the armies closed, the king of the Pandavas did a strange thing. Yudhishthira, eldest of the five brothers and the one they called the Just, took off his armour, set down his weapons, climbed from his chariot, and walked on foot toward the enemy, his hands joined. His brothers hurried after him, alarmed. "What are you doing?" Arjuna called. "Why do you leave your brothers and walk into the foe unarmed?" "Where will you go without your armour?" Bhima demanded. Nakula and Sahadeva pleaded with him too. But Yudhishthira said nothing and kept walking.

Krishna smiled and explained what the others could not see. "I know what he intends," he said. "He has gone to bow to his elders, Bhishma and Drona and Kripa and Shalya, who are fighting on the other side. It is told in the old histories that the man who honours his teachers and elders before a battle is sure of victory."

Across the field the Kauravas saw the king coming toward them unarmed, and a great jeering rose up. They waved their garments and shouted that Yudhishthira was a coward who had come in terror to beg Bhishma's protection, and they mocked him, his brothers, and Krishna too. Yudhishthira walked through the shower of insults as though through rain, passed between the ranks bristling with arrows, and stood before the grandsire.

Seizing Bhishma's feet with both hands, he said, "I salute you. It is against you that we will fight. Give us your leave, and give us your blessing."

Bhishma's answer silenced the jeering ranks. "If you had not come to me like this," he said, "I would have cursed you, for you were bringing defeat upon yourself. I am pleased with you, my son. Fight, and win. Ask me for whatever boon you wish."

And when that courtesy was done, Krishna went to Karna on the open field. Karna was the one warrior of the enemy host who could match Arjuna. The world knew him as a charioteer's son, raised by the charioteer and his wife Radha, yet he fought like a king, and Duryodhana, the Kaurava king, had made him his friend. For the sake of the Pandavas, Krishna made him an offer. "I have heard it said, Karna, that out of your hatred of Bhishma you will not fight," Krishna said. "Come over to our side, son of Radha, and stay with us as long as Bhishma is not slain."

It was a strange offer, made in the open field between two armies: the finest warrior of the enemy invited across, and spared the one fight that burned in him. Karna heard it to the end. Then he answered, with no hesitation in it. "I will not do anything that is disagreeable to Dhritarashtra's son," he said. "However the war goes, whatever Bhishma thinks of me, Duryodhana is my friend and my king, and I will not be disloyal to him."

Krishna had come for the sake of the Pandavas, and he returned to them with the answer he had carried out with him: some loyalties are not bought, even with justice, even with a throne. The offer was made and refused, and the war would be fought with Karna on the side he had chosen. There was nothing left to do but begin.
reflection: Krishna's offer to Karna is war strategy in its purest form, but Karna's refusal is something rarer: a loyalty that no grievance could bend. He knows Bhishma despises him and that the Pandava cause is just, and still he will not do anything disagreeable to the man who stood by him when no one else would. Some bonds are chosen before they are reasoned about, and Karna honors his to the end.
tradition_note: This is the second offer Krishna makes to Karna; an earlier and fuller offer before the war is told elsewhere in the Mahabharata, when Karna's reasons for refusing are given at greater length.
next_story_tease: The war began, and by evening Bhishma's arrows would bring Yudhishthira to the edge of despair.
hero_scene: On the open field between the two armies, Krishna stands before Karna making his offer with an open hand, while Karna, tall and unbending in his armor, refuses with folded arms as the conches of both armies sound in the distance.
